name: Dashrath Manjhi
tagline: The man who moved a mountain with a hammer and chisel
story:
In 1959, Dashrath Manjhi's wife Falguni slipped while crossing the treacherous Gehlour hills near their village in Bihar, India. She was carrying his lunch to the fields. The fall injured her badly, and the nearest hospital was 70 kilometers away — because the mountain stood between their village and the town. She died. Manjhi, a landless laborer from the Musahar community, the lowest rung of India's caste hierarchy, decided that no one else would suffer the same fate.

The next morning, he picked up a hammer, a chisel, and a crowbar, and began cutting into the mountain. Alone. His neighbors called him a madman. His family pleaded with him to stop. The government ignored him entirely. But every single day for twenty-two years — from 1960 to 1982 — Manjhi woke before dawn and broke rock. He sold his goats to buy tools. He lived on almost nothing. When his chisels broke, he walked miles to buy new ones.

By 1982, he had carved a road 110 meters long, 9 meters wide, and 7.5 meters deep through solid rock. What once took a 70-kilometer detour now took one kilometer. Schools, hospitals, and markets became accessible to his entire village overnight. The government, embarrassed into action, finally paved the road after his death in 2007.

Manjhi once said, "When God doesn't answer your prayers, you do it yourself." He never waited for permission, funding, or recognition. He just swung the hammer — every day, for two decades — because one woman's death made him refuse to accept the mountain as permanent. The mountain disagreed. The mountain lost.
